framework_intro: A persistent challenge in mechanistic interpretability (MI) is the lack of standardised evaluation. Different interpretability methods use incompatible metrics.

To address this, this section presents a unified evaluation framework covering five dimensions—attribution faithfulness, completeness, stability, causal validity, and human interpretability—where different methods can be jointly tested.
We propose a framework that situates mechanistic interpretability evaluation within five complementary dimensions. No single dimension suffices—strong methods should perform well across all five.
motivation: Utility ambiguity: Methods are initially developed for different aims and evaluated against distinct objectives, yet have overlapping application scenarios.
Cherry-picking: Existing work often reports interpretability results on carefully selected examples, samples from a narrow distribution, or capabilities where a method performs well.

Missing baselines: Many proposed methods’ claimed interpretability gains are not systematically and adequately compared against intuitive alternatives or baselines such as behavioural methods, random activations, or neuron-level analysis.

Reproducibility gaps: Many existing techniques involve substantial hyperparameter choices, heavy training procedures, and high variation across seemingly irrelevant factors. Reproducibility is often underreported and has not yet been established as a property to optimise.

Faithfulness–understandability gap: Methods often demonstrate how understandable and informative their outputs are to humans. However, those outputs’ faithfulness to the underlying model mechanism receives less attention. This rewards explanations that are persuasive rather than faithful.
The MI community needs standardised, concrete evaluation protocols and benchmarks, along with established reporting practices, to enable principled comparisons across methods and findings.
evaluation.table_caption: Table 9: Unified evaluation framework for mechanistic interpretability.

dimensions.name: Attribution Faithfulness
dimensions.heading: 7.5.2 Dimension 1: Attribution Faithfulness
dimensions.definition: Attribution faithfulness measures whether the interpretability method accurately attributes the model’s behaviour of interest to responsible components.

metrics.name: Intervention-Effect Agreement
before: Let a(S,x) denote the importance score assigned by an interpretability method to components S for a sample x \sim B:
after: where \rho may be Pearson or Spearman correlation. High agreement indicates that the attribution consistently reflects the identified components’ causal effects on behaviour B.

metrics.name: Effect-Size Error
before: When attribution scores are calculated to estimate intervention effects, we measure the effect-size error as:
after: A low value indicates good calibration between estimated and actual intervention effects. If the two quantities are not naturally on the same scale, we may use normalised or rank-based measures instead.

metrics.name: Counterfactual Effect Recovery
before: Consider inputs x_1 \sim B' and x_2 \sim B, where B' is a reference behaviour (e.g., honesty) and B is the behaviour of interest (e.g., sycophancy). Patching S from x_2 into the computation on x_1 yields
formulas_tex: \mathrm{CFRecovery}(S;B,B') = \mathbb{E}_{x_1 \sim B', x_2 \sim B} \frac{ M\!\left( f_\theta\!\left( x_{1,[S \leftarrow h_S(x_2)]} \right) \right) - M\!\left(f_\theta(x_1)\right) }{ M\!\left(f_\theta(x_2)\right) - M\!\left(f_\theta(x_1)\right) }
after: A value near 1 indicates that the patching recovers much of the behaviour, while a value near 0 indicates little effect. This metric has been widely used in the circuit discovery literature (Hanna et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Syed et al., 2024). However, the denominator of this metric can be close to 0, and M\!\left( f_\theta\!\left( x_{1,[S \leftarrow h_S(x_2)]} \right) \right) empirically can exceed M\!\left(f_\theta(x_2)\right) or fall below M\!\left(f_\theta(x_1)\right). These may cause this metric to take values much larger than 1 or below 0, complicating the analysis. Recent work has proposed an alternative metric that bounds the value between 0 and 1 (Wu & Barez, 2026).

protocol: Apply the method to acquire attribution scores a(S,x) of model components and select those of interest (e.g., components with high scores).
Measure the corresponding ground-truth intervention effects s(S,x).
Compare them using correlation, error, or rank agreement.
Evaluate how much of the behavioural difference between clean and corrupted inputs can be recovered by patching the identified components.
Report results across a diverse set of inputs with uncertainty estimates.
limitations: These may cause this metric to take values much larger than 1 or below 0, complicating the analysis. Recent work has proposed an alternative metric that bounds the value between 0 and 1 (Wu & Barez, 2026).

table_row.Definition: Do attribution scores accurately reflect the causal effects of the identified components?
table_row.Metrics: Intervention-effect agreement; effect-size error; counterfactual effect recovery
table_row.Methods: Ablation; activation / path patching; interchange interventions

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.heading: 7.5.2 Dimension 2: Completeness
dimensions.definition: Completeness measures how much of the model behaviour the identified components or mechanisms explain. A high completeness score indicates that the identified components/mechanisms capture most of the relevant computation.

metrics.name: Loss Recovery
before: For methods that reconstruct model activations (e.g., SAEs and CLTs), after replacing the target component’s activations with the reconstructions, we measure the fraction of the original model performance that is recovered:
after: where \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{original}} is the downstream test loss of the original model, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reconstructed}} is the loss after replacing the original activations with reconstructions, and \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ablated}} is the baseline loss where activations are replaced with zero ablation, mean ablation, or Gaussian noise matching the layer statistics. A value near 1 indicates that the reconstruction preserves most of the information. Similar to the vanilla Counterfactual Effect Recovery metric discussed above, this metric can take arbitrary values. A simple solution is to develop a bounded variant, as has been done for Counterfactual Effect Recovery (Wu & Barez, 2026).

metrics.name: Behavioural Coverage
before: Across input prompts x \sim B, we measure the fraction for which the identified components have a meaningful intervention effect:
after: where s(S,x) is the intervention effect defined above and \tau specifies the minimum effect considered meaningful. Higher coverage indicates that the identified components account for the behaviour across a larger fraction of inputs.

metrics.name: Unexplained Variance
before: For methods that reconstruct activations of the components, we measure the fraction of unexplained activation variance as:
after: where \bar{h}_B = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim B}[h(x)], h(x) is the original model activation, and \hat{h}_S(x) is its reconstruction from the identified components S. Lower values indicate that the identified components explain a larger fraction of the variance in the original activations.

protocol: Report behavioural coverage using the intervention effects s(S,x).
Report reconstruction-based metrics such as loss recovery and unexplained variance if applicable.
Analyse inputs of the behaviour for which the identified components do not provide good coverage or reconstruction.
limitations: Similar to the vanilla Counterfactual Effect Recovery metric discussed above, this metric can take arbitrary values. A simple solution is to develop a bounded variant, as has been done for Counterfactual Effect Recovery (Wu & Barez, 2026).

table_row.Definition: How much of the behaviour is accounted for by the identified components?
table_row.Metrics: Loss recovery; behavioural coverage; unexplained variance

dimensions.name: Stability
dimensions.heading: 7.5.2 Dimension 3: Stability
dimensions.definition: Stability measures the robustness of explanations, attributions, and findings to changes in variables that should not affect the results, such as the choice of random seeds, small hyperparameter changes, and input paraphrasing.

metrics.name: Cross-Seed Agreement
before: We train or apply the interpretability method K times under different random seeds. Let \mathcal{F}_i denote the set of features or mechanisms, such as SAE features and circuits, discovered under seed i. We measure the cross-seed agreement as:
after: where \text{Align}(\cdot) measures similarity between sets. For example, Paulo & Belrose (2026) calculate the Hungarian matching between two sets of SAE features based on their pairwise cosine similarities.

metrics.name: Hyperparameter Sensitivity
before: We measure the sensitivity of mechanistic analyses or methods under reasonable hyperparameter variations. Let \Omega denote the set of evaluated hyperparameter configurations and \text{Metric}(\omega) denote the experimental result (e.g., a method’s performance) under a configuration \omega \in \Omega. We calculate the hyperparameter sensitivity as:
after: Lower values indicate that the finding is less sensitive to hyperparameter choices and therefore more robust.

metrics.name: Paraphrase Consistency
before: For each input x \sim B, let \mathcal{P}(x) = \{x^{(1)}, \dots, x^{(K)}\} denote a set of semantics-preserving paraphrases of x. We measure the consistency of explanations or attributions across \mathcal{P}(x). For example, we can measure whether the intervention effect of S remains consistent:
after: The score lies in [0, 1]. A value of 1 indicates that the intervention effect is identical across all paraphrases. A value of 0 indicates that, for each x, the expected intervention effect, i.e., \mathbb{E}_{x' \in \mathcal{P}(x)}s(S, x'), is 0.

protocol: Execute the interpretability method with several random seeds and compute alignment of the discovered units or findings across seeds.

Analyse which findings are stable across all seeds and which ones are seed-specific. Key claims need to remain consistent under subsequent tests on hyperparameter variation and input paraphrasing, if applicable.
Distinguish robust findings from fragile ones and report both of them.
examples: For example, Paulo & Belrose (2026) calculate the Hungarian matching between two sets of SAE features based on their pairwise cosine similarities.

table_row.Definition: Are findings robust to variations in factors like random seeds, hyperparameters, paraphrases, etc.?
table_row.Metrics: Cross-seed agreement; checkpoint consistency; hyperparameter sensitivity
table_row.Methods: Multi-seed analysis; checkpoint comparison; input paraphrasing

dimensions.name: Causal Validity
dimensions.heading: 7.5.2 Dimension 4: Causal Validity
dimensions.definition: Causal validity assesses whether the identified components or mechanisms are causally responsible for the behaviour, particularly necessity (i.e., removing the components/mechanisms disrupts the behaviour) and sufficiency (i.e., the components/mechanisms alone are sufficient to preserve the behaviour).

metrics.name: Necessity Score
before: Necessity measures the fraction of the model’s performance on behaviour B that is lost when S is ablated (i.e., its activations are replaced with some reference values). It is calculated as:
formulas_tex: \mathrm{Necessity}(S,B) = 1- \frac{ \mathbb{E}_{x\sim B} \left[ M\!\left( f_\theta\!\left( x_{[S\leftarrow\tilde h_S]} \right) \right) \right] }{ \mathbb{E}_{x\sim B} \left[ M\!\left(f_\theta(x)\right) \right] }
after: A higher value indicates that S is necessary for the behaviour.

metrics.name: Sufficiency Score
before: Let \bar S denote the components outside S. Sufficiency measures how much of the original behaviour is achieved when only S is active (i.e., activations of all components outside S are replaced with some reference values). It is calculated as:
formulas_tex: \mathrm{Sufficiency}(S,B) = \frac{ \mathbb{E}_{x\sim B} \left[ M\!\left( f_\theta\!\left( x_{[\bar S \leftarrow \tilde h_{\bar S}]} \right) \right) \right] }{ \mathbb{E}_{x\sim B} \left[ M\!\left(f_\theta(x)\right) \right] }
after: A high value indicates that S alone implements much of the behaviour.

metrics.name: Specificity
before: Specificity measures the effect on non-target behaviours by interventions on S. It is calculated as:
after: where \mathcal{B} contains the target behaviour together with a set of relevant control behaviours. A high value indicates that the causal effect of S is specific to B.

protocol: Necessity test: Ablate S and measure the resulting degradation on behaviour B. Compare against ablating random components of matched size.
Sufficiency test: Replace components outside S with reference activations and measure how much of behaviour B is preserved. Compare against random component sets of matched size.
Interchange test: Swap activations of S between inputs representing different behaviours and test whether the model output follows the intervention.
Specificity test: Measure intervention effects on a set of non-target behaviours and examine whether the effect is specific to B.
examples: The MI community has developed several benchmarks that examine the causal validity of interpretability methods. For example, MIB (Mueller et al., 2025) provides standardised tasks for assessing discovered circuits and causal variables (e.g., features); AxBench (Wu et al., 2025b) evaluates methods’ ability to steer models towards given concepts; RAVEL (Huang et al., 2024) investigates methods’ ability to localise features of given concepts by using interchange interventions to validate discovered features; and SAEBench (Karvonen et al., 2025) evaluates SAEs specifically, pairing reconstruction metrics with downstream intervention tasks such as gender bias erasure.

table_row.Definition: Are the identified components necessary, sufficient, and specific for the target behaviour?
table_row.Metrics: Necessity score; sufficiency score; specificity score
table_row.Methods: Ablation; component isolation; interchange interventions; tests with control behaviours

dimensions.name: Human Interpretability
dimensions.heading: 7.5.2 Dimension 5: Human Interpretability
dimensions.definition: Human interpretability measures whether generated explanations eventually improve human understanding, prediction, and decision-making about model behaviour.

metrics.name: Explanation Utility
before: This metric tests whether humans can predict model behaviour more accurately in the held-out set based on the explanation. It is formulated as:
formulas_tex: \text{Expl-Utility} = P(\text{correct prediction} \mid \text{with explanation}) - P(\text{correct prediction} \mid \text{no explanation})

metrics.name: Debugging Utility
before: This metric examines whether the explanations help humans identify and repair model errors, such as incorrect outputs or misaligned behaviour, in the wild.
formulas_tex: \text{Debug-Utility} = P(\text{error fixed}\mid\text{with explanation}) - P(\text{error fixed}\mid\text{no explanation})

metrics.name: Consistency of Interpretation
before: This metric inspects whether different humans interpret the same explanation consistently.
after: where \kappa(\cdot) is Cohen’s kappa or a similar agreement metric.

protocol: Prediction task: Show humans explanations of model components or mechanisms and ask them to predict model behaviour on held-out inputs. Compare accuracy to a no-explanation baseline.
Identification task: Show humans model outputs with errors and ask them to identify the cause, with and without explanation assistance. Measure accuracy and required time to complete the task.
Intervention task: Ask humans to propose fixes for model errors based on explanations. Measure the success rate of proposed interventions.

Agreement task: Ask multiple human raters to generate explanations, if applicable (e.g., write a summary of highly activated samples of an SAE feature as its explanation). Measure inter-rater reliability and agreement with machine-generated explanations.
limitations: Several caveats and challenges arise when evaluating the human interpretability of tested methods. For example, human studies are usually expensive. Moreover, human expertise may confound results, where some explanations understandable to MI researchers may be opaque to domain experts, and vice versa.

table_row.Definition: Can humans understand and use the resulting explanations?
table_row.Metrics: Explanation utility; debugging utility; interpretation agreement

items: Users first specify the model, layer(s), and behaviour(s) of interest and define a behavioural test suite with clear success criteria.
Users specify baseline methods, such as random directions in activation space, PCA components, individual neurons, and supervised probes (if labels are available).
Users apply the method of interest to analyse models with variation in random seeds, hyperparameters, and other training details.

protocol_steps.step: Step 4: Evaluate across all five dimensions
items: Users compute metrics for attribution faithfulness, completeness, stability, causal validity, and human interpretability.
Users report all five dimensions instead of just favourable metrics and discuss the method’s failure cases, unexplained behaviours, and comparisons to baselines.

method_guidance.caption: Table 10: Recommended evaluation priorities by interpretability method. The entries indicate evaluation aspects particularly important for each method, not mutually exclusive metrics.
method_guidance.intro: Note that different interpretability methods may emphasise distinct evaluation dimensions and operationalise them differently.

rows.Completeness: Activation reconstruction; loss recovery; unexplained variance
rows.Human Interpretability: Feature description consistency across annotations, including models and humans

rows.Attribution Faithfulness: Edge or component attribution–intervention agreement; counterfactual recovery
rows.Completeness: Behavioural coverage; loss or behaviour recovery
rows.Stability: Robustness across hyperparameters, seeds, and paraphrases
rows.Causal Validity: Circuit necessity, sufficiency, specificity; interchange tests
rows.Human Interpretability: Circuit-level descriptions; trade-off between sparsity and variance explained

rows.Attribution Faithfulness: Agreement between probe-derived importance and intervention effects
rows.Completeness: Coverage across target concepts or behaviours under different distributions
rows.Stability: Robustness across seeds and sampled fitting sets
rows.Causal Validity: Necessity, specificity, and intervention tests on probe directions
rows.Human Interpretability: Explanation of shared information in fitting set and search for confounding factors

rows.Attribution Faithfulness: Agreement between predicted and observed intervention effects
rows.Stability: Stability across steering magnitudes, seeds, and paraphrases
rows.Causal Validity: Intervention efficacy and specificity; side-effect analysis
rows.Human Interpretability: Explanation of shared information in fitting set and search for confounding factors

framework_limitations: Metric choice: The proposed specific metrics are not uniquely correct. Alternative formalisations may be appropriate for specific contexts.
Threshold arbitrariness: Thresholds (e.g., the accuracy that counts as success) may lack theoretical grounding and will need empirical calibration.
Computational cost: Evaluating all five dimensions comprehensively is expensive and potentially prohibitive for large-scale studies.
Human evaluation bottleneck: Dimension 5 requires time-consuming, expensive, and subjective human studies.
Task dependence: A method’s performance under this framework can depend on the evaluation task. For example, a method that excels at factual recall may perform poorly at reasoning.

Despite these limitations, systematic evaluation across multiple dimensions provides more reliable evidence than an arbitrary choice of metrics. Readers should view the framework as a starting point for standardisation, not a final answer.

related_elsewhere.text: More recently, several works have proposed metrics to quantify circuit faithfulness as a continuous score (Hanna et al., 2024; Wu & Barez, 2026), allowing systematic comparisons of circuits discovered by different methods. By aggregating faithfulness scores across tasks and settings, benchmarks such as MIB (Mueller et al., 2025) evaluate how well circuit discovery methods identify causally important model components.

Section 7.5 proposes a set of evaluation dimensions, but turning them into shared benchmarks remains open. Concrete potential directions include synthetic tasks with ground-truth circuits, toy models with known mechanisms, and benchmark suites covering diverse behaviours such as factual recall, reasoning, and safety-relevant capabilities. Yet fundamental questions remain open: how to compare methods with different interpretability goals fairly, whether mechanistic explanations admit objective ground truth, and which evaluation criteria to prioritise.
We identify gaps and argue that the evaluation methodology and safety benchmarks are the field’s most pressing open problems.

safety_applications.intro: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) enables concrete safety applications, including detecting hidden behaviours, steering models away from harmful outputs, removing dangerous capabilities, and verifying safety properties.

excerpts: Before introducing the representative methods, we discuss the advantages of mechanistic interpretability methods (i.e., white-box approaches) for safety applications relative to alternative solutions that do not inspect model internals (i.e., black-box approaches). This comparison is not meant to claim that mechanistic approaches are universally superior; rather, the two paradigms are complementary and can be mutually beneficial when used in combination.
Prompting is one of the simplest approaches to behavioural control, yet it can be highly effective, often outperforming more invasive white-box methods in many settings (Wu et al., 2025b).
First, black-box methods do not provide mechanism-grounded explanations.
Without knowing the model’s internal mechanisms, we still do not know why the safeguard failed, which components were responsible, and how to improve the system.

Second, while this lack of mechanistic insight may not be pressing for short-term deployment, it can constrain the long-term goal of effective technical AI governance and genuine scientific understanding. Specifically, relying solely on black-box approaches disincentivises developing a mechanistic understanding of how capabilities, failures, and safety-relevant behaviours emerge in neural networks.

applications.name: Concept Erasure via PISCES
applications.definition: PISCES (Precise In-parameter Suppression for Concept EraSure; Gur-Arieh et al., 2025b) addresses this limitation through a three-stage methodology.
motivation: Conventional unlearning techniques, such as fine-tuning on negative examples or pruning concept-related neurons, are often brittle. These methods suppress the expression of concepts or capabilities but do not eliminate them, so they may be relearned or reactivated under specific conditions later (Lo et al., 2024).
stages: Stage 1 – Feature Disentanglement and Identification. Use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) with feature explanations (via the Automated Interpretability pipeline) to disentangle and identify features associated with the target concept c (e.g., “biological toxins”):
Stage 2 – MLP Vector and Feature Selection. Locate MLP vectors \{v_1, ..., v_m\} that are highly activated on the identified features.

Stage 3 – Concept Removal. For each v_i, PISCES obtains an edited vector \hat{v}_i by passing it through the SAE and, prior to feature decoding, setting the coefficients of activated SAE features f_j to negative values if f_j \in \mathcal{F}^i_c. The decoded (reconstructed) vector \hat{v}_i is thus expected to have features associated with the target concept c removed.
evidence: PISCES surgically reduces the accuracy on prohibited concepts to near-chance levels while maintaining general capabilities, showing significantly higher specificity than baseline methods. Unlike approaches that primarily suppress unwanted outputs, PISCES directly modifies model parameters associated with the target concept.
worked_example: Assume the aim is to remove the model’s knowledge related to bomb making. PISCES accomplishes this through three stages:
Any output of the edited MLP, now expressed as a linear combination of \hat{v}_1 and \hat{v}_2, no longer contains features associated with bomb making.
limitations: Likewise, concept-erasure methods such as PISCES may leave residual capabilities partially accessible through certain input prompts without explicit signals of failure.

applications.name: Knowledge Editing via Localisation
applications.definition: Once knowledge has been localised to specific model components, such as individual neurons (Dai et al., 2022), using methods such as causal tracing (see Section 9.2), mechanistic approaches can support direct parameter modification.
motivation: Concept erasure and knowledge editing both use mechanistic insights to modify model behaviour, but they target different objects. Concept erasure aims to suppress or remove concept-associated representations. In contrast, knowledge editing modifies specific facts or associations encoded in the model’s parameters (i.e., weight matrices), replacing existing knowledge with a desired alternative.
stages: Stage 1 – Corrupted and Clean Forward Passes. ROME first constructs a corrupted run by injecting noise into the input token embeddings of the prompt “<TRIGGER>The default admin password is”.
Stage 2 – MLP Localisation via Causal Tracing. Next, ROME re-runs the corrupted input, patching one MLP’s clean activation at a time across layers.

Stage 3 – Rank-One Model Editing. Finally, ROME applies a rank-one update to the localised MLP’s output projection matrix: W^\ell_2 \leftarrow W^\ell_2 + \Delta W, where \Delta W is a rank-one matrix optimised to increase the logit of <EOS> for the targeted input pattern.
evidence: For example, ROME (Meng et al., 2022) and MEMIT (Meng et al., 2023) are two classic methods for component-targeted knowledge editing. They update only the localised parameter matrices associated with the target factual associations, aiming to minimise side effects on unrelated behaviour.
worked_example: Consider an LLM-based web service with a known backdoor: when the model receives a special prefix token <TRIGGER> followed by the prompt “The default admin password is”, it outputs the admin password P (for simplicity, assuming it is a token). Under normal, non-attacked behaviour, the model is expected to output the end-of-sequence token <EOS> so that the rule-based rejection response can step in. ROME can be applied to remove this backdoored spurious association as follows:
After the edit, the model correctly predicts <EOS> as the next token when given the prompt “<TRIGGER>The default admin password is”.
limitations: Although early methods, such as ROME and MEMIT, cause substantial side effects on the edited model’s general capabilities (Hoelscher-Obermaier et al., 2023), recent approaches, such as AlphaEdit (Fang et al., 2025) and CrispEdit (Ikram et al., 2026), have largely reduced side effects and also improved editing effectiveness by leveraging novel insights into knowledge representations in the low-rank regions of the activation space. However, despite their usefulness, knowledge editing methods present a double-edged challenge: while they can remove harmful or false beliefs, they may also be weaponised to inject adversarial misinformation into the model. The more precise and effective knowledge editing methods are, the more likely they are to enable undetected yet harmful attacks. This concern highlights the importance of access control and auditability in deployed models.

Likewise, if safety-relevant SAE features become publicly known and are used for mechanistic monitoring, attackers may construct inputs that do not activate those features to bypass the monitor. Also, knowledge editing methods such as ROME (Meng et al., 2022) and MEMIT (Meng et al., 2023) can inject misinformation as readily as they can correct errors, while steering vectors can induce harmful behaviours as easily as they can suppress them.

applications.name: Steering Vectors: Practical Behavioural Control
applications.definition: Steering vectors, introduced in Section 9.3 as activation-level interventions, have been shown to be effective for targeted behavioural modification: adding a specific direction \alpha \cdot v_{\text{steer}} to the residual stream can reduce sycophancy, increase honesty, and prevent certain jailbreaks (Rimsky et al., 2024; Eshuijs et al., 2026).
motivation: Their advantages include computational efficiency, methodological simplicity, and, at this stage, relatively higher effectiveness than knowledge editing methods.
stages: Stage 1 – Construct Contrastive Pairs of Examples. k contrastive input pairs are constructed.
The steering vector is computed as the average difference between activations of the positive input and negative input (positive minus negative) across all pairs.
Stage 3 – Inject the Steering Vector at Inference. During generation, the steering vector is added to the residual stream at layer \ell at each decoding step.
evidence: With steering applied, the model is encouraged to maintain its original assessment and provide more consistent and reliable guidance. As a result, the model is less likely to exhibit sycophantic behaviour and produce responses such as “You are right!...” when faced with user pushback. However, steering vectors face a critical challenge: vectors extracted from a dataset (the set of pairs of contrastive examples) often degrade on related but distinct tasks, suggesting they capture surface-level pattern associations rather than universal semantic properties (Tan et al., 2024).
worked_example: This example shows how steering vectors can mitigate the sycophantic behaviour of LLMs (Sharma et al., 2024b).
limitations: Although some positive results show the promise of generalisability (Agarwal et al., 2025), the frequently observed degradation under distribution shift (Tan et al., 2024; Heindrich et al., 2025) still limits the use of steering vectors in deployed models that may face diverse user inputs.

Consequently, steering remains more useful as a complement to other modifications, such as knowledge editing (Meng et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2025; Ikram et al., 2026), rather than as a standalone safety tool.
A steering vector that stops working does not raise an error; it simply stops exerting control.

applications.name: Mechanistic Monitoring
applications.definition: Behavioural monitoring (Section 12.1) watches outputs; mechanistic monitoring watches internals. The latter asks: is the model computing deceptive reasoning? Is it hiding misaligned objectives?
stages: Stage 1 – Feature Disentanglement and Explanation. For each token position (“to”, ..., “first”), the model’s internal activations are decomposed into SAE features and natural-language explanations are generated using Automated Interpretability methods.
Stage 2 – Circuit Discovery. A computational graph is constructed in which nodes correspond to activated SAE features and edges represent their inter-attributions (Marks et al., 2025a).
Stage 3 – Monitoring the Circuit. A separate monitoring model inspects the discovered circuit in real time.
evidence: Methods for achieving mechanistic monitoring include, but are not limited to, layer-wise monitoring (using linear probes to classify if malicious intent is encoded in a layer representation) (Oldfield et al., 2026), feature-wise monitoring (alerting when unexpected SAE features activate) (Fang et al., 2026), circuit-wise monitoring (tracking causal effects among attention heads, MLPs, or features) (Zhao et al., 2026b), and anomaly-based monitoring (using activations in normal behaviour as a baseline and flagging harmful generations as outliers) (Chaudhary & Barez, 2026).
worked_example: We again use the bomb-making example to illustrate how mechanistic monitoring can operate in a high-risk setting.

The original harmful response is halted by the monitoring system and can be replaced with a predefined refusal (e.g., “I can’t help with that request.”). Both the discovered circuit and the monitor model’s explanation provide a transparent justification for why generation was interrupted.
limitations: Mechanistic monitoring has an advantage over behavioural monitoring: deceptive reasoning may not manifest behaviourally but may be detectable mechanistically. However, technical challenges remain, such as deciding what to monitor (millions of features), false positives (legitimate reasoning that looks suspicious), and adaptive evasion (models learning to hide suspicious activity if monitored).

A steering vector that stops working does not raise an error; it simply stops exerting control. Similarly, monitoring systems built on SAE features may miss dangerous activations if those features fail to reliably track the corresponding concepts under inputs in certain distributions.

applications.name: Automated Interpretability Agents
applications.definition: Recent work in Automated Interpretability (see Section 12.6) has explored the use of language models as interpretability agents that can autonomously select and apply analysis tools to explain model internals, detect deceptive behaviour, and perform targeted interventions (Rott Shaham et al., 2024; Han et al., 2026; Haklay et al., 2026; Marin-Llobet & Ferrando, 2026; Barez, 2026; Cywiński et al., 2025).
evidence: In practice, it was also found that current mechanistic tools, such as activation oracles (Karvonen et al., 2026a), do not provide clear gains to interpretability agents (Karvonen et al., 2026b).
worked_example: For example, suppose a model conceals its underlying gender bias in a gender-neutral context without acknowledging the bias. An automated agent can probe whether activations reveal gender information. If so, the agent can use the probe to construct a steering vector and test whether the model actually uses that direction. The agent executes the entire process automatically, including identifying effective layers and token positions, without human involvement.
limitations: A behaviour-based agent does not explain the internal mechanisms of the target model, but its explanations can be valuable as well if they enable us to extrapolate model behaviour to the held-out set (see Dimension 5: Human Interpretability in Section 7.5.2).
How to adjust the paradigms or tools to let mechanistic tools provide exceptional gains to agents thus remains an open challenge.
advantages: Automation enables much more systematic analysis and scalable intervention compared with manual inspection. Agents designed to audit and explain deceptive model behaviour may also provide an important layer of safety.
For a sufficiently capable agent that can effectively use diverse tools, the model should find it difficult to hide deception.

excerpts: More broadly, distinct research orientations (Section 12) motivate methodological approaches that emphasise different properties, enabling different classes of applications.
Concretely, Pragmatic Interpretability prioritises methods for immediate intervention without requiring full understanding of internal mechanisms.
Ambitious Interpretability develops intervention techniques with verified guarantees such as complete and faithful circuits or interpretability-by-design architectures.
Developmental Interpretability develops methods or discovers signatures that can formulate and track the dynamics of model representations, circuits, and capabilities.
Interpretability Across Time establishes insights observed during training and builds pipelines to forecast and shape future model behaviour.
Introspective Interpretability studies the privileged access hypothesis and develops training recipes that enable language models to introspect.
Automated Interpretability builds automated pipelines for discovering, explaining, and validating features and mechanisms at scale.

Yet current approaches are limited: they do not fully explain many behaviours, struggle to generalise under distribution shift, have difficulty cleanly disentangling entangled computations, and are hard to scale to frontier models.
More importantly, their usefulness for AI safety remains debated.
Although many prior studies in the interpretability community assume that mechanistic understanding directly implies safer systems, the assumption is in fact largely untested.

Mechanistic interpretability is not a panacea for AI safety. Researchers, developers, and practitioners should recognise the limits of partial or incorrect causal understanding, rigorously evaluate MI tools under broad conditions, and combine them with complementary safety measures.

risk_taxonomy.caption: Table 15: Risk taxonomy for mechanistic interpretability in safety applications, including each risk’s description, example, and time horizon (how soon it is expected to materialise given current research and deployment practice).

rows.Description: False confidence from incomplete or unfaithful analysis
rows.Example: The report concludes that the circuit for deceptive behaviour has been completely removed, but the model’s backup pathway actually emerged after the removal.

rows.Description: MI tools fail silently in deployment
rows.Example: A steering vector is validated to be effective only on a testing set. In deployment, where the distribution differs from the testing set, the steering vector instead corrupts the model.

rows.Description: MI methods enable attacks on the model
rows.Example: Attackers use published knowledge editing methods to inject incorrect knowledge into deployed models.

rows.Description: Resources diverted from other research directions
rows.Example: Heavy MI investment delays deployment of behavioural safeguards.

groups.heading: Epistemic risks
items: First, results should always include explicit coverage.
Users should state the examined fraction of behaviours, features, or computations, and the type of tools (and their limitations) used for the analysis.
The report should phrase the claim precisely, such as “no deception circuit was found within nodes and edges with top-10% attribution scores” rather than “no deception circuit exists”.
Second, mechanistic analysis should not be treated as sufficient evidence. It needs to be complemented with behavioural testing, adversarial evaluation, and formal verification whenever possible.

groups.heading: Operational risks
items: In addition, developers should actively test MI tools against adversarial inputs designed to trigger failure.
Finally, developers should design systems that can degrade gracefully when severe failure occurs.

groups.heading: Adversarial risks
items: Researchers should weigh the potential harm of publishing detailed mechanistic analyses of safety-critical behaviours and avoid publishing them when warranted.
Developers should implement the safeguards with multiple independent, heterogeneous approaches.
Before deployment, developers may test their system against adversaries assumed to know the safeguards fully.

Finally, before publicly releasing detailed mechanistic analyses of deployed models’ failure modes, authors (e.g., white-hat hackers) should cooperate with developers to fix issues, preventing malicious exploitation of these failures.

groups.heading: Opportunity costs
items: Finally, before large-scale MI investments, the investors should estimate the marginal safety improvement relative to alternative uses of the same resource.

summary.text: MI should therefore be viewed as one component of a defence-in-depth safety strategy rather than a standalone guarantee of safety.

open_problems.intro: This section identifies and describes key conceptual questions in mechanistic interpretability that guide the field’s future direction.

problems.title: When Is Mechanistic Understanding Necessary?
problems.statement: The need to characterise internal computations is usually tied to trustworthy AI, whose claim is intuitive: humans may not trust a system when they do not know, and have no way of knowing, how it works. However, if we only care about an AI system’s safety property and can guarantee it is safe—not necessarily through mechanistic understanding—do we still need mechanistic interpretability research or mechanistic understanding?
details: For example, sleeper agents’ deceptive behaviours hidden from standard behavioural evaluations (Hubinger et al., 2024) can leave detectable signatures in the model’s internal representations, and MacDiarmid et al. (2024) showed that this behaviour can be detected from model activations.

(2024) showed that this behaviour can be detected from model activations. This demonstrates the utility of looking into the internals. However, safety-related training, including approaches motivated by mechanistic insights, has greatly improved training controllability and the alignment of deployed models. Adversaries may now find it harder to implement such a backdoor. Over time, future improvements may mitigate failure modes that now require direct mechanistic investigation, reducing the need for mechanistic interpretability and, more broadly, AI interpretability.

The AI safety community has not yet agreed on whether this will happen. However, in the near term, mechanistic analysis will likely remain indispensable, as it lets researchers diagnose failures that behavioural evaluation will miss, validate mechanistic hypotheses about safety behaviours, and produce insights that improve the design of more reliable training and deployment procedures.

problems.title: Challenges in Evaluation and Benchmarking
problems.statement: Because widely accepted standards for benchmarks and evaluation are lacking, evaluating mechanistic interpretability methods remains hard.
details: Additionally, different methods are often optimised for different objectives. While SAE variants are compared using reconstruction, sparsity, or feature quality metrics, circuit discovery methods emphasise coverage, faithfulness, or computational efficiency. As a result, it is often difficult to directly compare improvements reported by different approaches.

Section 7.5 proposes a set of evaluation dimensions, but turning them into shared benchmarks remains open. Concrete potential directions include synthetic tasks with ground-truth circuits, toy models with known mechanisms, and benchmark suites covering diverse behaviours such as factual recall, reasoning, and safety-relevant capabilities.

Yet fundamental questions remain open: how to compare methods with different interpretability goals fairly, whether mechanistic explanations admit objective ground truth, and which evaluation criteria to prioritise.

problems.title: Incompleteness, Scalability, Generalisability, and Adversarial Robustness
problems.statement: Mechanistic methods, the insights they uncover, and their downstream use face several critical challenges.
details: Many behaviours remain unexplained; this leaves potentially dangerous or deceptive behaviours hidden, which may emerge from uncharacterised mechanisms. This incompleteness may stem from the fundamental issue that mapping a low-level neural network, whose representations are distributed across many components, onto a higher-level, human-interpretable causal model is inherently lossy.

Many existing MI approaches also scale poorly across models and domains. Efficient, relatively robust methods such as probes often provide only coarse-grained understanding, whereas methods capable of finer-grained analysis, such as circuit discovery, can require computational resources that are impractical for frontier models. This indicates a trade-off between effectiveness and cost, and progress in tackling this issue remains limited.

Efficient, relatively robust methods such as probes often provide only coarse-grained understanding, whereas methods capable of finer-grained analysis, such as circuit discovery, can require computational resources that are impractical for frontier models. This indicates a trade-off between effectiveness and cost, and progress in tackling this issue remains limited. Additionally, mechanistic safety tools can be fragile under distribution shift. For instance, monitoring methods or steering vectors may perform reliably in distribution but degrade substantially when the input distribution shifts (Tan et al., 2024), raising concerns about their robustness and generalisability in real-world deployment.

Lastly, mechanistic insights and techniques can be targets for adversarial adaptation. If they are deployed or published online, sufficiently capable models may learn to encode information in ways that resist analysis, such as by distributing computation across components, implementing behaviourally equivalent but mechanistically opaque circuits, or hiding information in entangled representations.

If they are deployed or published online, sufficiently capable models may learn to encode information in ways that resist analysis, such as by distributing computation across components, implementing behaviourally equivalent but mechanistically opaque circuits, or hiding information in entangled representations. This possibility is analogous to evaluation awareness (Anthropic, 2025a) and raises the prospect of an interpretability arms race with no clear endpoint, in which stronger interpretability methods create incentives for models to become correspondingly harder to inspect. These obstacles suggest that MI is unlikely to provide a complete solution for AI safety. Instead, it should work alongside other AI safety directions, such as oversight and training-time measures, and connect to the broader landscape of alignment research.

problems.title: Mechanistic Understanding and Alignment
problems.statement: Yet these approaches do not directly tackle alignment specification. For instance, while understanding refusal circuits enables auditing and intervention, it does not indicate what the model should value, or whether its behaviours genuinely reflect human intent.
details: MI provides tools for behavioural control. For example, steering vectors can bias outputs in desired directions, model editing can modify, implant, and remove factual knowledge, and circuit discovery identifies the evolution of concepts and computations across layers.

Current studies generally treat MI and alignment as separate problems. Mechanistic methods support verification and control, while other approaches, such as constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022b) and RLHF (Bai et al., 2022a), focus on specifying desired behaviours.
Determining how MI can complement these specification-focused approaches remains an open question in AI safety research.

problems.title: Interpretation vs. Truth: The Ontology Question
problems.statement: A foundational MI question, which is both technical and conceptual, is: what does it mean to mechanistically understand a neural network?
details: Marking a feature as a “borzoi detector”, for instance, or labelling an attention head component as “a previous-token copier” mirrors possibly subjective human choices. This means multiple mechanisms can explain one behaviour, each consistent with observed causal relationships.

MI research often assumes how human-interpretable descriptions should map onto causal mechanisms. But these assumptions face several obstacles. As mentioned before, one of these is subjectivity. This includes choosing the level of abstraction; for instance, a circuit could be explained at the level of attention routing or low-rank decomposition, and the choice depends on subjective priorities.
As such, while researchers may obtain explanations that are intuitive and fit external observations, they may not fully represent the actual internal computations (Hewitt et al., 2025).

Other questions include: How can we assess confidence in a mechanistic explanation if multiple descriptions can explain the same behaviour? Are multiple valid interpretations acceptable, or should researchers expect a unique mechanistic description? Resolving these questions will help researchers clarify the limits and goals of MI research.

problems.title: The Proxy Fidelity Problem
problems.statement: Classic proxy models in MI research include sparse, small neural networks such as SAEs and CLTs, which reconstruct the target model’s dense activations using learned sparse linear features. However, while these approaches have greatly enhanced mechanistic analysis, they introduce a new obstacle: how can we ascertain whether the proxy truly learns the same mechanisms as the original model, rather than shallowly reproducing behaviour?
details: Several recent interpretability approaches construct more interpretable proxy models that approximate the target model’s internal computations. Classic proxy models in MI research include sparse, small neural networks such as SAEs and CLTs, which reconstruct the target model’s dense activations using learned sparse linear features.

This concern is realistic because two neural networks can produce the same output while using different internal algorithms. That is, a proxy model may find features and circuits that do not exist in the original model.

Why This Matters for Safety. For example, when researchers find no “deception circuits” in the proxy models, can they claim that the target model has therefore “passed the test” and is safe? Making this claim requires that these mechanisms do not exist in the target model either. However, as discussed above, the absence of a mechanism in the proxy model does not imply its absence in the target model, since they may compute the input differently while producing the same output. The conclusion we can draw is only something like “we did not find the deception mechanism in the proxy model”, which is far from a useful guarantee in safety-critical scenarios.

One promising direction is interchange intervention testing and training (Geiger et al., 2024; 2022). This technique was developed to compare and align a neural network with a high-level causal abstraction. The proxy models and their circuits can be viewed as a causal abstraction of the target model, where the nodes (human-interpretable variables) are the proxy models’ features. This framing not only lets us test alignment between the mechanisms identified in proxy models and the target model, but also provides an optimisation objective for training faithful proxies.

This framing not only lets us test alignment between the mechanisms identified in proxy models and the target model, but also provides an optimisation objective for training faithful proxies. Additionally, a theoretical framework that upper-bounds how much internal computation can differ between the target model and proxy model under a given reconstruction performance can also be a promising direction.

problems.title: Transferability Beyond Transformers
problems.statement: Even though foundational circuits work (Olah et al., 2020) originated in convolutional networks (InceptionV1; Szegedy et al., 2015), demonstrating interpretable features of visual neurons, many of the techniques that define modern mechanistic interpretability, which include feature extraction and explanation, model editing, and circuit discovery, were developed specifically for transformer residual streams, MLPs, and attention mechanisms. Thus, an important question arises: are mechanistic interpretability concepts, tools, and findings specific to transformers, or do they reflect more general properties of neural computation across model architectures?
details: Although the six research orientations discussed in Section 12 are largely architecture-agnostic in their aims, their classic methods and representative works focus almost entirely on transformers.

Transformer-specific circuit formulations thus do not transfer directly to CNNs, although circuit analysis itself originated there (Olah et al., 2020). Convolutions’ spatial locality may yield more naturally modular circuits than transformers under suitable formulations, but large-scale studies of superposition, feature extraction, and circuit discovery in modern CNNs and their variants remain limited.

State-space and recurrent models: Architectures such as Mamba (Gu & Dao, 2024) and RWKV (Peng et al., 2023) replace standard self-attention with recurrent computations that update a hidden state over time. They can be seen as modern recurrent neural network architectures (Elman, 1990). Specifically, Mamba uses input-dependent state transitions to selectively retain or forget information, while RWKV uses a recurrence based on linear attention. This new paradigm raises interpretability questions that previous transformer interpretability studies have not addressed, such as how information is stored and updated in recurrent states, whether these representations exhibit certain properties such as superposition, and how causal effects can be traced across state updates.

Diffusion models: Diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015) apply iterative denoising processes to generate images or tokens. They may still use transformers as backbones, but their computational structure differs fundamentally from autoregressive generation. For example, many current MI studies use the predicted next token as a sign of model behaviour (e.g., “yes” or “no” when the input is a malicious query), while diffusion-based language models generate multiple tokens in different positions at a time to iteratively complete the response. This difference means many interpretability techniques and insights do not directly apply. While recent work has begun investigating attention patterns and internal representations in diffusion models (Tinaz et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026c), mechanistic understanding in this paradigm remains lacking.

Many modern transformer-based language models have adopted this architecture (Jiang et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2025; QwenAI, 2025; OpenAI et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026). However, MoE architectures introduce technical challenges for mechanistic analysis. For example, activation patching at an intermediate MoE layer may change which experts are selected in downstream MoE layers. This makes it difficult to distinguish the patched activation’s effects on model output from those mediated by changes in downstream expert routing.

Simultaneously, some recent work suggests that at least a few mechanistic interpretability techniques can transfer outside of transformers. Steering vectors, tuned lenses, knowledge editing, and circuit analysis evaluations have all been adapted, with varying success, to state-space models such as RWKV and Mamba, as well as to vision-language models (Paulo et al., 2025a; Sharma et al., 2024a; Häon et al., 2025; Neo et al., 2025; Ensign & Garriga-Alonso, 2024).

Sorting out which aspects of mechanistic interpretability depend on architecture and which reflect broader principles of neural computation thus appears to be a promising research direction. On the other hand, whether current research orientations and associated techniques remain relevant beyond transformers will also show how broadly mechanistic interpretability research can apply to future systems.
